bib.title: Measuring the Effects of Data Parallelism on Neural Network Training

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed; appendix figure axis text (plot ticks) is noise and was not read line by line.

question: How does batch size (the amount of synchronous data parallelism) affect the number of training steps needed to reach a goal out-of-sample error, what governs it, and does large batch cost solution quality?
contributions: Steps-to-result vs batch size has the same three-regime form (perfect scaling, diminishing returns, maximal data parallelism) across six model families, three optimizers and seven data sets, with learning rate, momentum and schedule tuned per batch size
Maximum useful batch size varies widely; momentum extends it vs plain SGD; model matters in non-simple ways; data set matters less and not through size
Optimal metaparameters do not follow linear or square-root learning-rate scaling heuristics
Disagreement in the literature on large-batch solution quality is largely explained by metaparameter tuning and compute-budget protocol; public database of training curves

method.summary: For each workload (model, data set, optimizer) and each batch size, the authors ran quasi-random metaparameter search (learning rate, momentum, decay schedule, label smoothing) and recorded the fewest training steps to first reach a fixed goal validation error. They compared batch sizes under step budgets and epoch budgets to separate batch size from compute budget.
method.task: Measuring steps-to-result vs batch size for supervised image classification and language modelling

datasets.name: ImageNet
datasets.preprocessing: random S in [256,512] aspect-preserving resize, random 224x224 crop, horizontal flip, mean RGB subtraction; eval resize 256 and central crop 224

datasets.name: Open Images v4
datasets.preprocessing: 7,186 trainable classes; only human-annotated positives, all others negative; same as ImageNet

datasets.name: LM1B
datasets.preprocessing: sub-word tokenizer, vocab 32,000; training sentences clipped to first 64 tokens (about 2% affected); no clipping at eval (max 476)

datasets.name: Common Crawl
datasets.split: 99.98% train / 0.02% holdout; first 6,075 holdout sentences as validation
datasets.source: Common Crawl June 2017 archive, filtered as Anil et al. 2018
datasets.preprocessing: vocab 24,006 sub-word tokens; clipped to 64 tokens train, 476 eval

models.name: Fully Connected (FC-N1-...-Nk)
models.architecture: ReLU MLP, dropout 0.4 on hidden layers; sizes varied (e.g. FC-1024, FC-128-128-128 to FC-2048-2048-2048)

models.name: Simple CNN (base/narrow/wide)
models.architecture: 2 conv layers (5x5, stride 1, same padding) with 2x2 max-pool, 1 FC layer, dropout 0.4
models.hidden: base 32/64 filters, 1,024 FC units; narrow 16/32, 512; wide 64/128, 2,048

models.name: ResNet-8
models.architecture: 7 conv layers with residual connections plus 1 FC; He et al. 2016a n=1 with improved block; no batch norm

models.name: ResNet-50
models.architecture: 49 conv layers with residual connections plus 1 FC; ghost batch norm with ghost batch size 32; label smoothing tuned

models.name: VGG-11
models.architecture: 8 conv layers plus 3 FC; Simonyan and Zisserman model A

models.name: LSTM
models.architecture: one hidden-layer LSTM, simpler variant of Jozefowicz et al. 2016 LSTM-2048-512; no output bias
models.hidden: 1,024 embedding dims, 2,048 hidden units, 512 projection dims

models.name: Transformer (base/shallow/narrow and shallow/wide)
models.architecture: Vaswani et al. 2017 decoder used as autoregressive LM; base as in original; shallow = 2 hidden layers instead of 6; narrow and shallow = half hidden units, heads and filter size; wide = double
models.context: sentences clipped to 64 tokens at training

training.objective: Cross-entropy / softmax loss for classification (sigmoid for Open Images), next-token cross-entropy for LM; label smoothing on ResNet-50 and optionally MNIST/Fashion MNIST
training.optimizer: Mini-batch SGD, SGD with momentum, Nesterov momentum (default Nesterov); TensorFlow MomentumOptimizer update rules; LSTM on LM1B used fixed gamma=0.99
training.lr: tuned independently at every batch size by quasi-random search (search ranges shown in Figs 9, 10, 13, 14, not given as numbers in text)
training.lr_schedule: constant for Fully Connected, Simple CNN, Transformer, LSTM; linear decay from eta0 to alpha*eta0 over T steps for ResNet-8, ResNet-50, VGG-11 (chosen after Appendix C comparison on ResNet-50/ImageNet)
training.warmup: null: not used in the main experiments; paper only mentions warmup as a technique others use
training.batch_size: swept as powers of two, e.g. 1 to 2^16 depending on workload (Fig 1 axes)
training.steps: measured outcome (steps to goal); budgets used in Sec 4.8: 5k to 5000k steps (MNIST), 10k to 1000k (LM1B); Fig 10 budget 50,000 steps; Fig 9b 25,000 steps; Appendix C 150,000 steps
training.epochs: epoch budgets in Sec 4.8: 10 to 10000 epochs (MNIST), 0.2 to 20 (LM1B); Fig 9a budget one epoch
training.seq_len: 64 tokens training clip (LM1B and Common Crawl)
training.dropout: 0.4 on Fully Connected hidden layers and Simple CNN FC layer
training.regularisation: label smoothing (values {0,0.01,0.1} for b<=2^14 and {0,0.1} above on ResNet-50; {0,0.1} on MNIST/Fashion MNIST); ghost batch norm 32; tried L2 and gradient noise unsuccessfully
training.compute: over 25 hours of wall time for each metaparameter configuration in saturation runs (Sec 3.2.1 footnote and Sec 4.8)
training.seeds: no repeated seeds; the best trial among 100 (or 50) non-divergent quasi-random trials per batch size is reported

other.metaparameter_search: quasi-random search (Bousquet et al. 2017), equal budgets of non-divergent trials per batch size; 100 non-divergent trials generally, 50 for Transformer Shallow on LM1B with SGD, Transformer on Common Crawl and LSTM on LM1B; search space re-run if optimum near boundary or goal not reached
other.goal_errors: MNIST simple CNN 0.01; Fashion MNIST 0.1; CIFAR-10 ResNet-8 0.3; ImageNet ResNet-50 0.25; VGG-11 0.35; Open Images AP 0.31; LM1B and Common Crawl Transformer 3.9 cross entropy; LSTM LM1B 3.9
other.scale: database of 454 workload-batch size combinations, 168,160 models, 71,638,836 loss measurements

inference.samples: one best trial out of 50-100 per batch size; no repeated runs

metrics.name: Steps to result
metrics.definition: fewest training steps at which any metaparameter trial first reaches a goal validation error

metrics.name: Average precision (Open Images)
metrics.definition: class-agnostic AP over all classes using area under discrete PR curve (tf.metrics.auc, 200 thresholds)

metrics.name: Cross entropy error
metrics.definition: average per-token cross entropy over a data set (log of per-token perplexity)

baselines: plain mini-batch SGD vs SGD with momentum vs Nesterov momentum
perfect-scaling line (steps halve per batch doubling)
linear and square-root learning-rate scaling heuristics
eval.protocol: Steps to result per batch size with independently tuned metaparameters; error goal varied modestly to check robustness (Fig 2); training error checked (Fig 12); solution-quality study under step or epoch budgets taking best validation checkpoint across all trials (Sec 4.8). No significance tests.

results.claim: Steps to reach a goal validation error fall proportionally with batch size at first, then show diminishing returns, then stop changing, in every workload.
results.setup: Nine workload panels in Fig 1: six model families, seven data sets, per-batch-size tuned metaparameters, Nesterov momentum by default

results.claim: The perfect-scaling regime ended at a batch size anywhere from 2^4 to 2^13 depending on the workload.
results.quote: ended anywhere from a batch size of 24 to a batch size of 213

results.claim: The maximum useful batch size (beyond which steps stop falling) varied between roughly 2^9 and 2^16.
results.quote: varied between roughly 29 and 216 in our experiments

results.claim: For ResNet-8 on CIFAR-10, perfect scaling ends at batch size 16 with plain SGD but Nesterov momentum extends it to batch size 256.
results.setup: ResNet-8 without batch norm, CIFAR-10, goal validation error 0.3
results.quote: Our experiments conﬁrmed that perfect scaling ends at batch size 16 with plain mini-batch SGD
results.note: The Nesterov value 256 is on the next line of the text: 'using Nesterov momentum extends the perfect scaling regime to batch size 256 (see Figure 1c)'.

results.claim: Momentum optimizers extend the perfect-scaling region to larger batch sizes than plain SGD but match SGD at small batch sizes; Nesterov and heavy-ball momentum differ little.
results.setup: Simple CNN on MNIST, Transformer Shallow on LM1B, ResNet-8 on CIFAR-10 (Fig 4)
results.quote: momentum optimizers perform identically to SGD without momentum

results.claim: No evidence that larger batch sizes degrade out-of-sample error; solution quality depends on compute budget (step vs epoch) more than on batch size.
results.setup: Simple CNN on MNIST and Fashion MNIST, Transformer (narrow shallow and base) on LM1B, 100 trials per batch size (Fig 11)
results.quote: subject to a budget on training steps, larger batch sizes achieve better out-of-sample error than smaller batch sizes, but subject to a budget on training epochs, smaller batch sizes achieve better out-of-sample error than larger batch sizes

results.claim: Optimal effective learning rate generally rises with batch size but does not follow linear or square-root scaling, sometimes decreasing; learning rate and momentum should be tuned jointly.
results.quote: it did not always follow either a linear or square root scaling heuristic

results.claim: Label smoothing improved ResNet-50 ImageNet validation error by up to about one percentage point at large batch sizes and had no apparent effect at small ones.
results.setup: ResNet-50 on ImageNet, fixed compute budget per batch size, smoothing in {0,0.01,0.1} (Fig 7)
results.quote: improved the error by as much as one percentage point

results.claim: Without label smoothing the 0.25 ImageNet error goal could not be reached for batch sizes above 2^14 within the training budget.
results.quote: Without label smoothing, we could not achieve our goal validation

results.claim: Narrower Transformers on LM1B scale to larger batch sizes than wider ones; ResNet-50 scales further than VGG-11 on ImageNet; Transformer further than LSTM on LM1B.
results.setup: Fig 3, y-axis normalised, goal errors chosen so all variants reach them
results.note: Quote is a fragment; the sentence continues 'allow Transformer to make more use of larger batch sizes on LM1B.'

results.claim: Data set effect on maximum useful batch size is smaller than model and optimizer effects and does not follow data set size consistently.
results.setup: Figs 5 and 6: MNIST vs Fashion MNIST, ImageNet vs Open Images, LM1B vs Common Crawl, and data subsets
results.quote: these diﬀerences are not simply as straightforward

results.claim: Saturating performance even on MNIST took millions of steps at small batch sizes or thousands of epochs at large ones, up to 25 hours per configuration.
results.setup: Simple CNN on MNIST and Fashion MNIST, 100 metaparameter configurations per batch size
results.quote: training for up to 25 hours per conﬁguration

results.claim: About 100 non-divergent quasi-random trials per batch size sufficed for stable steps-to-result.
results.setup: Per batch size and workload; 50 trials for Transformer Shallow/SGD on LM1B, Transformer on Common Crawl, LSTM on LM1B
results.quote: but 100 trials seemed to suﬃce in

results.claim: Released database holds 71,638,836 loss measurements for 168,160 models across 35 workloads.
results.quote: a database of 71,638,836 loss measurements taken over the course of training for 168,160

limits: Search spaces were specified by hand and may not suit every batch size; learning rate decay schedule searches were hard to verify as sufficient (Sec 5.1)
Smaller batch sizes got more validation measurements and so more chances of a lucky value; larger batch sizes that missed the goal got revised search spaces
Reports only the best trial; robustness across trials (e.g. median) and repeated seeds are not studied
Only SGD, momentum and Nesterov momentum; no Adam or second-order optimizers; no model parallelism
Results are retrospective: no way offered to predict the maximum useful batch size without tuning at every batch size
Idealised data parallel hardware assumed: step count as the time proxy, communication cost ignored
Width/depth effects inconsistent across architectures; dataset-size effect equivocal
Does not show the role of gradient noise scale; later work (not in this paper) addresses prediction

terms.definition: the number of steps needed to first reach a desired out-of-sample error
a data set, model, and training algorithm jointly
architectural choices and training parameters such as learning rates and regularization weights (the authors' name for hyperparameters)
eta_eff = eta/(1 - gamma), the contribution of a given mini-batch gradient to final parameters under momentum
region where steps needed halve for each doubling of batch size (b-fold benefit)
batch size beyond which increasing the batch size no longer changes the steps needed

lineage.note: linear LR scaling heuristic the paper tests and finds not general
concurrent work with the same three-region form but inconsistent results, attributed to LR heuristics
width claim not confirmed; narrow Transformers scaled better
reproduced ResNet-8 CIFAR-10 SGD result, perfect scaling ends at 16, extended by momentum
large-batch generalisation gap attributed to protocol and tuning

lineage.work: Chelba et al. 2014 LM1B; Anil et al. 2018 Common Crawl processing

figures.caption: The relationship between steps to result and batch size has the same characteristic form for all problems.
figures.why: Shows the three regimes (perfect scaling, diminishing returns, maximal data parallelism) in nine workloads at once.

figures.caption: Some models can exploit much larger batch sizes than others.
figures.why: Compares architectures and widths/depths on normalised axes.

figures.caption: Momentum extends perfect scaling to larger batch sizes, but matches plain SGD at small batch sizes.
Optimal effective learning rates do not always follow linear or square root scaling heuristics.
Validation error depends on compute budget more than batch size.
figures.why: Step budgets favour large batch, epoch budgets favour small.

code.snippet: eta_eff = lim_{T->inf} sum_{u=tau}^{T} eta*gamma^(u-tau) = eta/(1 - gamma)
eta_t = eta_0 - (1-alpha)*eta_0*t/T if t <= T ; alpha*eta_0 if t > T
